accuracy.evidence: Facts checked against the National Curriculum in England Year 6 geometry statement (recognise angles where they meet at a point, are on a straight line, or are vertically opposite, and find missing angles) and its Year 5 notes (straight line 180°, full turn 360°), and against Euclid Elements I.13 and I.15 for the proof given in the adult text (a + b = 180° and b + c = 180° so a = c). Every number in the lab, items and quiz was recomputed: 180 − 40 − 75 = 65, 180 − 90 − 35 = 55, 180 − 128 = 52, 360 ÷ 3 = 120, 360 − 95 − 110 − 85 = 70, 180 − 48 = 132; parameter ranges keep every answer positive (p3 minimum 90°, m2 minimum 40°, m4 minimum 60°, m7 only 3 to 6 equal angles so each answer is a whole number).

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented Year 6 slips seen in Year 6 angle work: 360° used on a straight line (chips 245°, 235°, 232°; quiz 295° and 270°; m5 Dan's 320°); 180° used round a point (quiz −110°, quiz 60° for three equal angles); adjacent angles assumed equal (chips 75°, 35°, 128°; scene 4 adjacent taps; quiz 38° vs 142°); subtracting from 90° (chip 38°, quiz 25° and 52°); giving the total of the known angles (chips 115°, 125°, quiz 290°); reading an angle by eye (reason card 'It looks about the same size', m6, quiz 7); and using 'round a point' before enough angles are known (scene 5 refusal).

lab_distinct.evidence: The lab is built on this topic's three angle facts and the act of justifying them: a ray turned on a line with a live a + b readout, missing-angle chips that each embody a named slip, three draggable rays that must share a full turn equally, a turning crossing whose yellow angle's partner must be tapped, and reason cards that are accepted or refused depending on what is already known. The lab-distinct gate passes under 30% with every flagship lab, including flagangle (types of angles), flagprot (protractor), flagtriang (triangle sums) and flagslide (transformations); none has reason cards or a turning crossing.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner discovers each fact before the text states it: turning the ray to three positions shows the total never moves from 180°; making three rays equal forces 360 ÷ 3; tapping partners while the crossing turns (55°, 120°, 70° rounds) shows opposite angles stay equal at every slope; in scene 5 'vertically opposite' is refused for b (it is adjacent) and 'round a point' is refused until two angles are known, so the learner sees which fact fits when. Each done message (LEARNT) then names the rule.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab then disproves: 'It changes as the ray turns' (the a + b readout stays 180° in every position); '180°, like a straight line' for angles round a point (the live total reads 360° however the rays move); 'The one right next to it' for the equal angle at a crossing (tapping a neighbour reveals a different size and the 180° pairing).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven challenge questions with wrong answers keyed to specific slips; slip() returns a distinct message for each: 'full' (used 360° on a line), 'line' (used 180° round a point), 'same' (adjacent assumed equal), 'add' (gave the total of known angles), 'ninety' (took away from 90°), 'quarter' (90° each is four angles, not three), 'adjopp' and 'oppnext' (mixed up opposite and next-door angles), 'oppb', 'early' and 'look' (judged by eye; diagrams not to scale).

readability.evidence: Kid text FK grade 2.2 and adult text 4.9 by learn/readability.py (limits 6.5 and 9.5 for a learner lesson). Sentences are short, use the Year 6 terms the curriculum expects (straight line, round a point, vertically opposite, full turn, half turn) and give one worked number per fact (180° − 130° = 50°, 360° ÷ 3 = 120°). Canvas prompts stay under 12 words, such as 'Which angle equals the yellow one?'.

no_filler.evidence: Every kid paragraph states one fact with a worked example; the adult text gives curriculum placement, the two-line proof, the list of common mistakes with a question to ask, and what the lab does. No filler phrases (content gate passes), and the explanation is under 12% similar to every other lesson, including 505 types of angles and 914 angles in triangles.

mobile.evidence: Checked on 390 px screenshots of all six steps, both mid-task and finished, plus a 1200 px dark-theme set: the diagram, angle labels, 4 number chips and 4 reason cards are readable without clipping; knobs are 13 px radius on phones with 44–48 px grab distance; real pointer drags on a 390 px viewport moved the ray, dragged chips and reason cards onto the diagram, turned ray B and tapped crossing sectors, each giving the expected spoken feedback. Narrow labels sit further out on angles under 60° so they clear the lines.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button twin (turn the ray 20°, '? = 65°' chips, ray A/B/C ↺ ↻ 15°, 'Angle b/c/d' and turn-line buttons, one button per reason) with descriptive aria-labels; the canvas aria-label is updated with each spoken result (for example 'a and c are vertically opposite: both 55°'). The pipeline walkthrough completed every task with Show me on desktop and iPhone 13, showed the challenge, and axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) found no violations in light or dark theme, with no console errors.

NCETM (2020) Primary mathematics guidance (ready-to-progress criteria), geometry and angle facts
